planting.note: Plant container-grown or grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Prok needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade while young, moving the tree toward full sun once it reaches fruiting age. Prok is one of the long-established named pawpaw selections that, alongside cultivars such as Sunflower, Overleese, and Mitchell, has been evaluated for decades in university and private pawpaw collections and is frequently used as a dependable pollinator and parent tree in breeding programs because of its vigorous growth and consistent production. Fruit is medium to large with smooth, custard-textured flesh and good, well-balanced sweet flavor typical of the species' banana-mango-vanilla character. As with all pawpaws, Prok is self-incompatible, so plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby and consider hand-pollinating with a small brush during the brief maroon-flowered bloom period to maximize fruit set.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown or grafted trees in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Supermom needs a genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, shifting toward full sun once the tree reaches fruiting maturity. Supermom is one of the Indiana-origin seedling selections made by longtime pawpaw collector Jerry Lehman, the same breeding line that produced other widely grown named cultivars such as Mango, Marshmallow, and IXL, and it earned its name for unusually heavy, reliable annual fruit set. Fruits are medium-sized with rich, smooth, custard-like flesh and good sweet flavor typical of the species. Because pawpaws are self-incompatible, plant a second, unrelated cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, and hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief spring bloom window to further improve fruit set in home orchard plantings.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program
